title: Environmentally friendly synthesis of quantum dots and their applications in diverse fields from the perspective of environmental compliance: A review.

sections.heading: Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs
sections.text: Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs The solvothermal method represents an efficient and rapid approach for synthesizing highly crystalline and monodisperse InP QDs. This synthetic route involves the introduction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling effective bandgap engineering. However, the method requires high temperature and Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explosion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stability. These QDs exhibited small particle sizes, tunable within the range of 2.5–3.7 nm, achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temperature modulation resulted in a bandgap tuning range of approximately 0.4 eV within the visible spectrum. The established methodology for InP QDs synthesis serves as a valuable reference for fabricating other III-V semiconductor QDs. Nozik et al. further employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [ 51 ]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvothermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor offers significant advantages over P(TMS)₃, being both less toxic and more cost-effective, aligning with the principles of green chemistry and sustainable material synthesis [ 52 ]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-friendly, and low-cost precursors to synthesize InP/ZnS core-shell QDs with tunable fluorescence properties through the green solvothermal method, achieving an impressive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [ 53 ].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis conditions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to industrialization. In the future, synergistic breakthroughs in performance and sustainability should be realized through reaction path innovation, precise structure regulation and green process iteration.

sections.heading: Heating method for the preparation of inp QDs
sections.text:
Heating method for the preparation of inp QDs The heating method is a reliable and scalable technique for colloidal nanocrystal synthesis, which enables controlled nucleation and crystal growth by dissolving precursors and ligands in solvents and initiating reactions by heating. By optimizing the precursors, stabilizers and heating rate, high quality nanocrystals comparable to thermal injection can be produced. However, the decomposition of ligands (e.g., oleylamine) at high temperatures releases amine gases that irritate the respiratory tract. These gases participate in photochemical reactions to form secondary pollutants such as ozone. Rapid nucleation is also prone to causing lattice distortion and high defect densities in QDs. To mitigate environmental impact, solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine) can be recovered via distillation or adsorption techniques, enabling closed-loop production. Figure  4 a illustrates the fundamental process of nanocrystal formation in heated synthesis and its correlation with the reaction vessel temperature [ 54 ]. Pidluzhna et al. employed the heating method to prepare core-shell InP/ZnS hybrid QDs, as depicted in Fig.  4 b Their study focused on the applicability of these synthesized InP/ZnS core-shell QDs in the stepwise fabrication of inverted solar cells, utilizing a combination of thermal vacuum deposition and spin-coating techniques [ 55 ]. Wang et al. developed cadmium-free InP/ZnSeS/ZnS thick-shell QDs using the heating method. By varying the number of zinc sources, they controlled the emission wavelength of the InP core and optimized the thickness of the ZnS layer, thereby enhancing the quality of the QDs [ 56 ]. Kim et al. reported a simple one-pot heating method for synthesizing InP and InP/ZnS core-shell QDs. By precisely controlling the flow rate and crystal growth temperature, they successfully synthesized high-quality InP/ZnS QDs with tunable emission wavelengths ranging from blue-green to red [ 57 ].Summarizing, the heating method in the synthesis of InP-based QDs exhibits the advantages of controllable core-shell structure construction, precise emission wavelength tuning, and highly efficient synthesis in a one-pot method. However, the limitations such as unresolved environmental risks, insufficient defects control, and poor process scalability are generally present. In the future, further breakthroughs can be achieved by developing bio-based ligands to replace oleylamine and coupling distillation/adsorption to achieve closed-loop production, introducing gradient shell layers and post-processing passivation to reduce the defect density, as well as combining microfluidic continuous-flow synthesis with machine-learning optimization of parameters.

sections.heading: Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs
sections.text:
Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs The hot-injection method achieves the separation of nucleation and growth phases by dissolving the precursor in organic solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine, and trioctylphosphine) by heating and injecting another precursor several times at a specific temperature to trigger the transient supersaturation of the solution, which allows for the homogeneous nucleation and controlled growth of crystals, and the products are both monodispersed and homogeneous; the variety of the choice of the reaction solvents and active agents further expand the product system [ 34 – 58 ]. However, the volatilization/decomposition of solvents at high temperatures (> 300 °C) releases volatile organic compounds (VOCs) (amines, alkanes, etc.), which causes air pollution and health risks, and requires secondary treatment of the exhaust gases and waste liquids. For example, Jamshidi Zavaraki et al. employed a hot injection method to synthesize colloidal InP and ZnS-covered InP QDs, which were successfully applied for the first time as sensitizers in quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSSCs) [ 59 ]. However, the stability of colloidal InP QDs was lower and the sensitivity to moisture is higher, so ZnS coating was used in this work to enhance the stability of InP and to protect InP QDs from moisture and interaction with electrolytes. Song et al. first introduced of high-quality InP QDs by the reaction of P(N(CH 3 ) 2 ) 3  hot injected at 220 °C with In and Zn chlorides dissolved in the relatively weakly coordinated solvent oleylamine, and achieved an unprecedented series of controlled synthesis of bandgap-tunable InP QDs, successfully achieving nucleation/growth of QDs (Fig.  5 ) [ 60 ]. Ramasamy et al. prepared InP/ZnS core-shell QDs using the hot injection method, and in this experiment, it was found that the presence of a small amount of water as an impurity not only significantly reduced the FWHM and increased the QY of InP/ZnS QDs [ 61 ]. InP/ZnS QDs obtained using In precursors and the presence of water in the solvent had a narrow FWHM of 46 nm and a high QY of 45%. In comparison, without water doping, the emission wavelength of the synthesized QDs was around 625 nm, with a FWHM of 66 nm and a QY of about 33% (its High Resolution Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) schematic of QDs synthesized with and without water was displayed in Fig.  6 ). Singh et al. successfully synthesized InP QDs and InP/ZnS core-shell structures using the hot injection technique. It was observed that the PL intensity increased gradually when the ZnS shell layer was increased, and the synthesized QDs were treated with HF to remove the defects on the surface of QDs and thus enhanced the luminescence intensity [ 62 ]. Hot injection method shows multiple breakthroughs in the synthesis of InP QDs. However, the method still suffers from limitations such as high-temperature decomposition of solvents, unidentified mechanism of water impurity enhancement, and strong corrosive waste liquid from strong acid treatment. In the future, we need to focus on the development of low-toxicity solvents to replace oleylamine, establish a quantitative model of water content and defect states to stabilize the process, and explore green defect passivation techniques such as photo/thermal annealing.

 Fig. 6 TEM images of InP core QDs synthesized ( a ) with and ( d ) without water. TEM and HR-TEM images of InP/ZnS core-shell QDs synthesized ( b ,  c ) with and ( e ,  f ) without water [ 61 ] 
 In addition to the aforementioned common preparation methods, alternative approaches such as ion exchange and crystal growth techniques, have been developed. The ion exchange system (Fig.  7 ) addresses the limitations of conventional crystal preparation methods and has emerged as a superior alternative for fabricating semiconductor nanostructures with phases that are challenging to obtain through direct chemical synthesis [ 63 ]. In this method, guest ions in organic or aqueous solvents replace cations in the host material, facilitating rapid ion exchange among Group II-VI, I-VI, and IV-VI semiconductors while preserving the original nanoparticle size and morphology. Moreover, this preparation procedure does not require expensive experimental equipment or specialized laboratory conditions [ 64 – 65 ]. For instance, Friedfeld et al. investigated the cationic doping behavior of InP clusters with Zn²⁺ and Ga³⁺ [ 66 ]. They identified the mixed alkyl carboxylic acid cluster Zn₅(Et)₄(OAc)₆ as the most effective zinc precursor, while both Ga(OAc)₃ and [Ga(CH₃)₂(MA)]₂ exhibited comparable doping activity. Shan et al. synthesized monodisperse InP QDs with a substabilized feldspathic zincite structure through a cation exchange reaction between Cu₃P nanocrystals and In precursors in the presence of tri-n-octylphosphine [ 67 ]. By adjusting the size of Cu₃P nanocrystals, size-tunable fibrillated zincite InP QDs were obtained (as shown in Fig.  8 ), demonstrating excellent optical properties. The crystal growth process involves separating nucleation and crystal growth into two distinct steps [ 68 ]. In the first step, a homogeneous solution containing seed crystals is prepared. In the second step, the seed crystal solution is mixed with the quantum dot precursor solution at room temperature. Finally, the mixture undergoes segmented flow processing at a temperature lower than the initial seed crystal formation temperature to ensure controlled crystal growth. This approach represents a significant advancement in achieving controlled QD synthesis with a narrow size distribution. Enright et al. successfully synthesized InP nanoparticles with a particle size of 3.0 nm using this crystal growth method. Their work also demonstrated that the crystal seed growth technique can be employed to synthesize tetrahedral nanostructures, and nearly any seed crystal with an accessible (111) plane can be grown in the direction of tetrahedral prisms. This methodology not only encompasses cubic core structures but also extends to (111) planar distorted quadrilateral lattices [ 69 ].

sections.heading: Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs
sections.text:
Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs The top-down approach allows direct physical or chemical access to large-area graphene arrays into GQDs with nanometer dimensions, controlling the shape, size, and growth direction of GQDs, and is suitable for large-scale production. However, the insufficient controllability of the size and shape of QDs prepared by this method, the serious surface defects and structural damages of QDs, the low efficiency of large-scale production, the high cost and energy consumption as well as the biocompatibility of nanoparticles limit their applications in medical fields. The top-down method presents diversified technological paths in the synthesis of GQDs, such as Samra et al. used coke as a raw material (with low impurities and high carbon content) to produce GQDs by a facile process (Fig.  9 a), and spectroscopic characterization verified the feasibility [ 77 ]. Xie et al. synthesized highly crystalline monodispersed bluish N-GQDs by nitrogen-containing 3D nanocarbon electrochemical cutting (Fig.  9 b), with a QY of 19.3% and nitrogen doping of 12.3%, combining both economic and green advantages [ 78 ]. Zhou’s team innovated acid vapor cutting of bulk nitrogen-doped carbon films (1 ml of nitric acid) and in situ filtration to obtain water-soluble blue-green photoresponsive N-GQDs (1.5–3.7 nm, Fig.  10 a), circumventing the tedious isolation step [ 79 ]. Tadyszak et al. demonstrated that the that the graphene oxide precursor preparation of GOQDs did not change the C/O ratio, and found 500 nm strong fluorescence dispersion and paramagnetism under 280–380 nm excitation (Fig.  10 b) [ 80 ]. Soriano et al. developed GQDs fluorescence for the detection of carbamates in water by using mixed-acid oxidation to modulate the reaction time (Fig.  10 c) [ 81 ].However, there are core limitations of this method, such as the strong corrosive waste liquid generated by the acid treatment method, the still low QY (< 20%) and the unclear mechanism of magnetic/optical property regulation. In the future, it could be attempted to develop green stripping technologies like laser/plasma to replace the strong acid process, construct doping-fluorescence-magnetism constitutive relationship models, and explore biomass carbon sources to reduce costs and increase efficiency.

sections.heading: Bottom-up Preparation method for the Preparation of GQDs
sections.text:
Bottom-up Preparation method for the Preparation of GQDs The bottom-up approach is to synthesize GQDs organically by the carbonization of organic molecules (e.g., citric acid, glucose, etc.) or polymers (the process is depicted in Fig.  11 ). The advantage of this method is that it is easy to control the shape and size of GQDs, which is an irreplaceable advantage in regulating the physical properties and molecular structure of substances. There are also certain disadvantages, such as the synthesis of large-size GQDs with many steps and cumbersome processes [ 82 ]. Prof. Chiang’s team investigated a bottom-up preparation method for the synthesis of colloidal QDs using an aqueous organosulfate solution treated with an atmospheric pressure argon (Ar) microplasma [ 83 ]. The average diameter of the fabricated colloidal GQDs was 4.9 nm, the QY was 1.5%, and the room temperature photoluminescence peak was 448 nm. Xu et al.used a top-down preparation method to synthesize GQDs with high solubility and excellent film-forming ability in common organic solvents. Significantly, this research not only solved the limitation of low solubility of GQDs prepared by traditional methods in organic solubility but also expected to successfully apply GQDs in other optoelectronic fields [ 84 ].Gao’s team applied a bottom-up synthesis method to prepare two water-soluble GQDs with different degrees of oxidation using graphene molecules, namely O-GQDs prepared by oxidation and R-QDs synthesized by reduction. The structural and compositional information of two GQDs, such as relevant functional groups, optical properties, structures, and molecular weights, was directly obtained through a series of characterizations, such as HR-TEM, Atomic Force Microscope (AFM), UV-vis spectroscopy, FL spectroscopy, and so on, to investigate their luminescence mechanisms [ 85 ]. Although the bottom-up method is novel and green, the current quantum efficiency is low; the top-down method is effective in solving the solubility problem, but has deficiencies in the complexity of the preparation process, etc. In the future, it is expected to optimize the preparation method to improve the quantum efficiency and further expand the applications in the field of optoelectronics.

Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs The top-down approach allows direct physical or chemical access to large-area graphene arrays into GQDs with nanometer dimensions, controlling the shape, size, and growth direction of GQDs, and is suitable for large-scale production. However, the insufficient controllability of the size and shape of QDs prepared by this method, the serious surface defects and structural damages of QDs, the low efficiency of large-scale production, the high cost and energy consumption as well as the biocompatibility of nanoparticles limit their applications in medical fields. The top-down method presents diversified technological paths in the synthesis of GQDs, such as Samra et al. used coke as a raw material (with low impurities and high carbon content) to produce GQDs by a facile process (Fig.  9 a), and spectroscopic characterization verified the feasibility [ 77 ]. Xie et al. synthesized highly crystalline monodispersed bluish N-GQDs by nitrogen-containing 3D nanocarbon electrochemical cutting (Fig.  9 b), with a QY of 19.3% and nitrogen doping of 12.3%, combining both economic and green advantages [ 78 ]. Zhou’s team innovated acid vapor cutting of bulk nitrogen-doped carbon films (1 ml of nitric acid) and in situ filtration to obtain water-soluble blue-green photoresponsive N-GQDs (1.5–3.7 nm, Fig.  10 a), circumventing the tedious isolation step [ 79 ]. Tadyszak et al. demonstrated that the that the graphene oxide precursor preparation of GOQDs did not change the C/O ratio, and found 500 nm strong fluorescence dispersion and paramagnetism under 280–380 nm excitation (Fig.  10 b) [ 80 ]. Soriano et al. developed GQDs fluorescence for the detection of carbamates in water by using mixed-acid oxidation to modulate the reaction time (Fig.  10 c) [ 81 ].However, there are core limitations of this method, such as the strong corrosive waste liquid generated by the acid treatment method, the still low QY (< 20%) and the unclear mechanism of magnetic/optical property regulation. In the future, it could be attempted to develop green stripping technologies like laser/plasma to replace the strong acid process, construct doping-fluorescence-magnetism constitutive relationship models, and explore biomass carbon sources to reduce costs and increase efficiency.

Bottom-up Preparation method for the Preparation of GQDs The bottom-up approach is to synthesize GQDs organically by the carbonization of organic molecules (e.g., citric acid, glucose, etc.) or polymers (the process is depicted in Fig.  11 ). The advantage of this method is that it is easy to control the shape and size of GQDs, which is an irreplaceable advantage in regulating the physical properties and molecular structure of substances. There are also certain disadvantages, such as the synthesis of large-size GQDs with many steps and cumbersome processes [ 82 ]. Prof. Chiang’s team investigated a bottom-up preparation method for the synthesis of colloidal QDs using an aqueous organosulfate solution treated with an atmospheric pressure argon (Ar) microplasma [ 83 ]. The average diameter of the fabricated colloidal GQDs was 4.9 nm, the QY was 1.5%, and the room temperature photoluminescence peak was 448 nm. Xu et al.used a top-down preparation method to synthesize GQDs with high solubility and excellent film-forming ability in common organic solvents. Significantly, this research not only solved the limitation of low solubility of GQDs prepared by traditional methods in organic solubility but also expected to successfully apply GQDs in other optoelectronic fields [ 84 ].Gao’s team applied a bottom-up synthesis method to prepare two water-soluble GQDs with different degrees of oxidation using graphene molecules, namely O-GQDs prepared by oxidation and R-QDs synthesized by reduction. The structural and compositional information of two GQDs, such as relevant functional groups, optical properties, structures, and molecular weights, was directly obtained through a series of characterizations, such as HR-TEM, Atomic Force Microscope (AFM), UV-vis spectroscopy, FL spectroscopy, and so on, to investigate their luminescence mechanisms [ 85 ]. Although the bottom-up method is novel and green, the current quantum efficiency is low; the top-down method is effective in solving the solubility problem, but has deficiencies in the complexity of the preparation process, etc. In the future, it is expected to optimize the preparation method to improve the quantum efficiency and further expand the applications in the field of optoelectronics. 
 Fig. 11 A diagram of the process of preparing QDs by bottom-up method [ 82 ]

Hot injection method for the Preparation of CIS QDs In the study of the synthesis of CIS QDs, hot injection is an effective means of preparing high-quality monodisperse QDs, but is limited by the scarcity of low-toxicity or nontoxic precursors. Zhu et al. applied a low-temperature hot injection preparation method to synthesize super-efficient green luminescent CIS QDs (the synthesis process appeared in Fig.  12 ). The introduction of S- Oil Amine (OAm)(S powder dissolved in ethylamine) as a sulfur precursor provided a large concentration of H 2 S at low temperature, which subsequently reacted chemically with Cu +  and In 3+ , leading to the explosive nucleation of CIS and the formation of CIS nuclei with smaller size and higher concentration [ 90 ]. Niyamakom et al. prepared ternary CIS QDs with particle sizes in the range of 7–14 nm using [Cu(acac) 2 ], [in (acac) 3 ], elemental sulfur and oleylamine (OLA) as raw materials, and investigated the effects of reaction time and precursors on the properties of the synthesized QDs. It was determined that the injection of elemental sulfur, [Cu(acac) 2 ], and oleylamine precursors in [In(acac) 3 ], respectively, initially formed a mixture of CuS nanoparticles, followed by a slow transformation to a tetragonal CIS phase (Fig.  13 ). The In content in the nanocrystals can be adjusted by changing the ratio of Cu: In precursors [ 91 ]. Liu et al. synthesized CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs using a hot injection method. Different ratios of PS-PE-BR-PS (SEBS) were used to blend with QDs to promote the dispersion of QDs, and finally a solution-based QDs/SEBS copolymer mixture was produced to form fluorescent films. The emission wavelengths and QY of CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs were 533 nm (84%) and 536 nm (97%), respectively. The emission wavelengths of CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al fluorescent films were classified as 574 nm, 582 nm, and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs fluorescent films with improved compatibility resulted in a luminescence efficiency of 51 lm/W [ 92 ]. Bao et al. fabricated monodisperse CIS nanocrystals by injecting mixed metal oleic acid (OA) precursors into hot organic solvents containing dissolved sulfur sources, such as OLA, 1-octadecene (ODE), OA, and their mixtures with dissolved sulfur sources. Different shapes of CIS nanocrystals were synthesized by changing the preparation conditions, such as triangular pyramids with tunable crystalline phases, bullet-like rods and conical anisotropic crystals [ 93 ]. Although the existing methods have made progress in morphology control, luminescence efficiency and dispersion improvement, they still face limitations such as high toxicity of precursors, complicated preparation process, and difficult to control the uniformity of components in large-scale production. Future research could focus on the development of environment-friendly precursors, optimization of the hot injection process to simplify the process and improve the reproducibility of production.

Introduction QDs technology’s impact has exceeded mere technological advances and is reinventing human lifestyles, economic models, and even civilization. In 1983, Brus et al. at Bell Laboratories first reported the quantum size effect in CdS nanocrystals, marking the inception of QDs research [ 1 ]. QDs is quasi-zero-dimensional semiconductor nanocrystals consisting of a small number of atoms that bind excitons in H-dimensional space, with a radius generally smaller than or close to the exciton bolometric radius, between 1 and 10 nm. The electronic structure exhibits a unique set of optoelectronic properties due to the change from a continuous energy level structure to a quasi-split energy level, i.e., with quantum-limited effects [ 2 – 4 ]. As (1) QDs can be tuned in size or structural composition, leading to spectral emission in the entire visible region [ 5 – 6 ]. (2) with a broad excitation spectrum and narrow emission spectrum, and its full width at half maximum (FWHM) is narrow [ 7 – 8 ]. (3) Excellent photostability [ 9 – 11 ]. (4) Long fluorescence lifetime, surface chemical plasticity, and good biocompatibility [ 12 – 13 ]. In addition, semiconductor colloidal QDs also have excellent properties such as solution processability and high color purity [ 14 ]. Currently, researchers have established a variety of mechanisms for QDs synthesis, which are divided into two main categories, namely physical preparation methods and chemical preparation methods [ 15 – 19 ]. The most common is chemical preparation, which is divided into two main methods: one is organic synthesis, and the other is synthesis in the aqueous phase [ 20 – 22 ]. Organic synthesis of QDs employs organometallic precursors (e.g., Cd(CH 3 ) 2 , Zn(CH 3 ) 2 ), which are highly unstable, sensitive to water and oxygen, toxic, flammable, and explosive, and the preparation process can only be carried out in a glove box filled with nitrogen. The process is complex and not suitable for large-scale production. Comparatively, the aqueous-phase synthesis is simple to operate and have a low cost. It requires no further modification, and QDs such as CdS, CdSe, and ZnSe have been successfully obtained in aqueous solution [ 23 – 26 ]. QDs has a high specific surface area with undercoordinated surface atoms, leading to pronounced surface defects that facilitate atomic aggregation and agglomeration, resulting in poor optical properties of QDs [ 27 ]. Over the years, researchers have made many efforts to eliminate the surface defects of QDs, the most common of which is to modify the surface of QDs using various organic and inorganic materials. The surface modification of semiconductor fluorescent QDs mainly includes inorganic shell layer passivation surface and functionalized group modification surface. For instance, Hines and Guyot-Sionnes first proposed to wrap 1–2 monolayers of ZnS shell layers on top of CdSe nanocrystals with a particle size of 3 nm, and eventually the quantum yield (QY) of QDs based on the CdSe/ZnS core-shell structure was enhanced to 50% [ 28 ]. Murcia et al. used acoustic chemistry driven synthesis of CdSe QDs and subsequently coated ZnS on the surface of CdSe QDs also by acoustic chemistry driven, with a QY of 50%-60% and FWHM of 25 nm [ 29 ]. Roy et al. reported a microwave-assisted synthesis of water-soluble CdSe/ZnS QDs with a maximum emission wavelength of 511 nm to 596 nm [ 30 ]. Functionalized groups modifying the surface of QDs commonly include organic small molecule modifications and organic polymer modifications, as Qian et al. combined experimental and theoretical approaches to systematically investigate the surface chemistry of a series of graphene QDs functionalized with small organic molecules. The surface functionalization of graphene QDs with alcohols, amines and thiols can effectively modulate the fluorescence of graphene QDs, and demonstrate that amines can significantly improve the QY of modified graphene QDs [ 31 ]. As shown in Figs.  1  and  2 , heavy metals in Cd-based QDs may be relatively harmful to the environment and living organisms, and in severe cases can lead to serious chronic diseases and cancers [ 32 – 33 ]. The UN Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reports that global electronic waste (e-waste) has surged to 62 million metric tons, with heavy metal emissions from this sector contributing 15–20% of the total industrial discharge. In response, multilateral environmental conventions have established a targeted governance framework, integrating legally binding protocols for toxic substance phase-outs. The Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment (1972) establishes foundational environmental rights and obligations under Principle 1: “Humankind bears the solemn duty to preserve intergenerational ecological integrity, entitling all to a healthy environment while mandating stewardship for future generations.” Principle 21 further codifies state responsibility to “prevent transboundary environmental harm through toxic substance control.” In accordance with this framework, the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development (1992) articulates the “Precautionary Principle” in Principle 15: “Where threats of serious or irreversible damage exist, scientific uncertainty shall not postpone cost-effective preventive measures, requiring states to implement anticipatory pollution controls through risk-weighted regulatory action and technology-forcing standards.” The Precautionary Principle prioritizes early intervention through legal norms enacted by public authorities to mitigate potential harm at its source. The jurisprudential essence of the precautionary principle is enshrined in the Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Project judgment (1997) by the International Court of Justice (ICJ):“Vigilance and prevention are non-derogable obligations in environmental governance, as ecological harm is characterized by irreversibility and remediation inherently constrained by scientific and technical limitations. This ruling underscores the imperative for anticipatory legal interventions, even amid epistemic uncertainty, to avert systemic risks posed by persistent pollutants. 1  For QDs not to cause harmful results in terms of environmental pollution, legal norms must actively take measures to prevent such damage and must ensure that these measures are effectively implemented, which is an environmental compliance obligation. The development of eco-friendly QD synthesis technologies aligns with green chemistry principles and fulfills the environmental compliance requirements of the precautionary principle.

 To date, eco-friendly QDs such as Indium Phosphide (InP) [ 34 – 35 ], graphene [ 36 – 37 ], CuInS 2  [ 38 – 39 ], Zn-based, etc., have also been developed to a large extent. For instance, InP QDs has superior features such as a larger exciton wave radius and high carrier mobility, stronger quantum confinement effect, wide spectral tunability, and larger intrinsic absorption coefficient, making them one of the excellent alternative materials for Cd-based QDs [ 40 – 41 ]. Yet, InP QDs also suffer from poor electron-binding ability, weak performance stability, and low QY. Graphene QDs, a new star in the family of carbon-based fluorescent nanomaterials, have received extensive attention from researchers globally in recent years [ 42 ]. Graphene QDs possess high chemical stability, upper fluorescence QY, strong resistance to photobleaching, lower cytotoxicity, and good biocompatibility. In addition, they also have significant photoluminescence properties, and fluorescence spectra with different emission wavelengths from the deep UV region to the IR region band can be obtained by changing the raw material ratios or synthesis pathways [ 43 – 44 ]. However, graphene QDs also often have broad emission peaks due to defective luminescence as well as poor carrier injection and low luminescence efficiency, limiting their more profound development in the field of illumination [ 45 – 47 ]. This paper first provides a comprehensive review of global regulatory frameworks governing heavy metal contaminants, particularly Cd, Hg, and Pb, with a focus on environmental compliance requirements in key jurisdictions, including the United States, the European Union, China, and Japan. The examination encompassed five critical dimensions: hazardous waste management protocols, production/usage restrictions, emission control standards, occupational safety regulations, and public right-to-know obligations. These legislative initiatives aim to mitigate heavy metal pollution through source control and exposure minimization, thereby directly driving the advancement of eco-friendly quantum dot alternatives. Building on global regulatory frameworks, this study analyzes three eco-friendly QDs—InP QDs, graphene QDs, and ternary CuInS 2  QDs by comparing their synthesis methods (hot injection, solvothermal, and thermal decomposition) and applications in optoelectronics, biomedicine, and environmental sensing. The analysis highlighted critical challenges: QY limitations (> 35% energy loss), ambient stability issues, and scalability constraints (± 15% batch variability). To address these issues, we propose machine-learning-optimized synthesis, atomic-layer encapsulation, and microfluidic production, ultimately envisioning hybrid architectures via plasma-enhanced doping to achieve > 95% quantum efficiency.

International and National regulatory frameworks governing heavy metal containment in QDs International convention The elimination of Cd, Pd, Hg, and their toxic and hazardous compounds at the sources of production, storage, trade, and transfer has been universally recognized in the formulation of many international conventions. An international convention is a written agreement between subjects of international law on mutual rights and obligations, which reflects the common will and interests of state parties [ 48 ]. As the development of international environmental issues will ultimately affect the alteration of the entire Earth’s ecosystem, their outcome is closely linked to the survival of human beings on Earth. In addition, emerging international environmental problems, such as holes in the ozone layer and transboundary waste transfer, cannot be solved by a single country and need to be regulated by multilateral international conventions of a global and regional nature [ 49 ]. As delineated in Fig.  3 , five pivotal conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Bamako, and Minamata) form the BRS + governance architecture. These regimes aim to collectively address the global challenges of heavy metal management by harmonizing standards to control the transboundary movement of hazardous substances and their impacts on human health and the environment. 
 Fig. 3 The BRS + governance architectures on the limitation of heavy metal 
 Non-compliant states primarily risk reputational damage or trade privilege revocation rather than coercive penalties, as evidenced by persistent non-compliance with the Stockholm Convention mandates on toxic substance phase-outs, where Cd-based QDs remain prevalent because of economic prioritization and technological path dependencies. For example, the Minamata Convention’s decade-long adoption timeline exemplifies how conflicting national interests (e.g., differentiated emission responsibilities between industrialized and developing economies) protract multilateral consensus building. 2.2 National legislation National legislation on heavy metal contaminants (Cd, Hg, Pb) emphasizes source control through production bans and import restrictions. As delineated in Table  1 , the United States implements prior informed consent (PIC) protocols, mandating dual obligations: exporter disclosure of chemical profiles for specified imports and consumer notification requirements for toxic substance-containing products. In contrast, the EU adopts preventative measures by limiting heavy metal concentrations in electronics and batteries while incentivizing safer alternatives through Horizon Europe funding mechanisms. Major economies, including China, Japan, and South Korea, operationalize three-phase regulatory models: (i) formal classification of Cd/Pb/Hg compounds as hazardous substances, (ii) manufacturing prohibitions coupled with product toxicity thresholds, and (iii) import control regimes targeting non-compliant goods. These frameworks demonstrate regulatory convergence in life-cycle management of toxic metals despite jurisdictional variations in implementation timelines.

Major economies, including China, Japan, and South Korea, operationalize three-phase regulatory models: (i) formal classification of Cd/Pb/Hg compounds as hazardous substances, (ii) manufacturing prohibitions coupled with product toxicity thresholds, and (iii) import control regimes targeting non-compliant goods. Eco-friendly QDs from an environmental compliance perspective With the enhancement of environmental awareness and the increasing strictness of environmental regulations, various industries are undergoing a transformation toward sustainable development. The development of eco-friendly QDs aligns with this trend, contributing to the sustainable development of quantum dot-related industries. By meeting market demands for the optical properties of quantum dot materials while reducing environmental impacts, it achieves a harmonious integration of economic growth and environmental protection. The advancement of eco-friendly QDs can drive the entire quantum dot industry to transition toward green and environmentally friendly practices, prompting relevant enterprises to research, develop, and adopt more sustainable production processes and materials. This encourages collaborative efforts across the entire industrial chain to improve resource utilization efficiency, reduce pollutant emissions, and enhance the overall environmental performance of the industry, thereby better addressing the challenges posed by increasingly stringent environmental regulations and market demands for eco-friendly products.Therefore, this section mainly summarizes the different environmentally friendly QDs synthesis methods and the corresponding environmental protection requirements for the development of QDs in modern society. InP QDs Recently, InP-based QDs has become one of the hot alternatives to Cd-based QDs due to their wide spectral range, similar optoelectronic properties with Cd-based QDs, and green environmental protection, thus attracting wide attention from researchers globally. Therefore, the synthesis and application of InP-based QDs will have an extremely important potential role in the future breakthrough of quantum dot display and lighting technology. Besides, eco-friendly InP QDs do not contain restricted substances such as Cd, Pb, Hg and fulfill the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS), Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), and other regulations. The development of eco-friendly InP QDs is a combination of “compliance dividend” and “green premium”, which creates long-term value for enterprises by reducing legal risks, gaining policy support, and enhancing market competitiveness. At present, the most usual methods for the synthesis of InP QDs are as follows; Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs The solvothermal method represents an efficient and rapid approach for synthesizing highly crystalline and monodisperse InP QDs. This synthetic route involves the introduction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling effective bandgap engineering. However, the method requires high temperature and Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explosion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stability. These QDs exhibited small particle sizes, tunable within the range of 2.5–3.7 nm, achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temperature modulation resulted in a bandgap tuning range of approximately 0.4 eV within the visible spectrum. The established methodology for InP QDs synthesis serves as a valuable reference for fabricating other III-V semiconductor QDs. Nozik et al. further employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [ 51 ]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvothermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor offers significant advantages over P(TMS)₃, being both less toxic and more cost-effective, aligning with the principles of green chemistry and sustainable material synthesis [ 52 ]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-friendly, and low-cost precursors to synthesize InP/ZnS core-shell QDs with tunable fluorescence properties through the green solvothermal method, achieving an impressive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [ 53 ].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis conditions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to industrialization. In the future, synergistic breakthroughs in performance and sustainability should be realized through reaction path innovation, precise structure regulation and green process iteration. Heating method for the preparation of inp QDs The heating method is a reliable and scalable technique for colloidal nanocrystal synthesis, which enables controlled nucleation and crystal growth by dissolving precursors and ligands in solvents and initiating reactions by heating. By optimizing the precursors, stabilizers and heating rate, high quality nanocrystals comparable to thermal injection can be produced. However, the decomposition of ligands (e.g., oleylamine) at high temperatures releases amine gases that irritate the respiratory tract. These gases participate in photochemical reactions to form secondary pollutants such as ozone. Rapid nucleation is also prone to causing lattice distortion and high defect densities in QDs. To mitigate environmental impact, solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine) can be recovered via distillation or adsorption techniques, enabling closed-loop production. Figure  4 a illustrates the fundamental process of nanocrystal formation in heated synthesis and its correlation with the reaction vessel temperature [ 54 ]. Pidluzhna et al. employed the heating method to prepare core-shell InP/ZnS hybrid QDs, as depicted in Fig.  4 b Their study focused on the applicability of these synthesized InP/ZnS core-shell QDs in the stepwise fabrication of inverted solar cells, utilizing a combination of thermal vacuum deposition and spin-coating techniques [ 55 ]. Wang et al. developed cadmium-free InP/ZnSeS/ZnS thick-shell QDs using the heating method. By varying the number of zinc sources, they controlled the emission wavelength of the InP core and optimized the thickness of the ZnS layer, thereby enhancing the quality of the QDs [ 56 ]. Kim et al. reported a simple one-pot heating method for synthesizing InP and InP/ZnS core-shell QDs. By precisely controlling the flow rate and crystal growth temperature, they successfully synthesized high-quality InP/ZnS QDs with tunable emission wavelengths ranging from blue-green to red [ 57 ].Summarizing, the heating method in the synthesis of InP-based QDs exhibits the advantages of controllable core-shell structure construction, precise emission wavelength tuning, and highly efficient synthesis in a one-pot method. However, the limitations such as unresolved environmental risks, insufficient defects control, and poor process scalability are generally present. In the future, further breakthroughs can be achieved by developing bio-based ligands to replace oleylamine and coupling distillation/adsorption to achieve closed-loop production, introducing gradient shell layers and post-processing passivation to reduce the defect density, as well as combining microfluidic continuous-flow synthesis with machine-learning optimization of parameters.

 Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs The hot-injection method achieves the separation of nucleation and growth phases by dissolving the precursor in organic solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine, and trioctylphosphine) by heating and injecting another precursor several times at a specific temperature to trigger the transient supersaturation of the solution, which allows for the homogeneous nucleation and controlled growth of crystals, and the products are both monodispersed and homogeneous; the variety of the choice of the reaction solvents and active agents further expand the product system [ 34 – 58 ]. However, the volatilization/decomposition of solvents at high temperatures (> 300 °C) releases volatile organic compounds (VOCs) (amines, alkanes, etc.), which causes air pollution and health risks, and requires secondary treatment of the exhaust gases and waste liquids. For example, Jamshidi Zavaraki et al. employed a hot injection method to synthesize colloidal InP and ZnS-covered InP QDs, which were successfully applied for the first time as sensitizers in quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSSCs) [ 59 ]. However, the stability of colloidal InP QDs was lower and the sensitivity to moisture is higher, so ZnS coating was used in this work to enhance the stability of InP and to protect InP QDs from moisture and interaction with electrolytes. Song et al. first introduced of high-quality InP QDs by the reaction of P(N(CH 3 ) 2 ) 3  hot injected at 220 °C with In and Zn chlorides dissolved in the relatively weakly coordinated solvent oleylamine, and achieved an unprecedented series of controlled synthesis of bandgap-tunable InP QDs, successfully achieving nucleation/growth of QDs (Fig.  5 ) [ 60 ]. Ramasamy et al. prepared InP/ZnS core-shell QDs using the hot injection method, and in this experiment, it was found that the presence of a small amount of water as an impurity not only significantly reduced the FWHM and increased the QY of InP/ZnS QDs [ 61 ]. InP/ZnS QDs obtained using In precursors and the presence of water in the solvent had a narrow FWHM of 46 nm and a high QY of 45%. In comparison, without water doping, the emission wavelength of the synthesized QDs was around 625 nm, with a FWHM of 66 nm and a QY of about 33% (its High Resolution Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) schematic of QDs synthesized with and without water was displayed in Fig.  6 ). Singh et al. successfully synthesized InP QDs and InP/ZnS core-shell structures using the hot injection technique. It was observed that the PL intensity increased gradually when the ZnS shell layer was increased, and the synthesized QDs were treated with HF to remove the defects on the surface of QDs and thus enhanced the luminescence intensity [ 62 ]. Hot injection method shows multiple breakthroughs in the synthesis of InP QDs. However, the method still suffers from limitations such as high-temperature decomposition of solvents, unidentified mechanism of water impurity enhancement, and strong corrosive waste liquid from strong acid treatment. In the future, we need to focus on the development of low-toxicity solvents to replace oleylamine, establish a quantitative model of water content and defect states to stabilize the process, and explore green defect passivation techniques such as photo/thermal annealing.

 In addition to the aforementioned common preparation methods, alternative approaches such as ion exchange and crystal growth techniques, have been developed. The ion exchange system (Fig.  7 ) addresses the limitations of conventional crystal preparation methods and has emerged as a superior alternative for fabricating semiconductor nanostructures with phases that are challenging to obtain through direct chemical synthesis [ 63 ]. In this method, guest ions in organic or aqueous solvents replace cations in the host material, facilitating rapid ion exchange among Group II-VI, I-VI, and IV-VI semiconductors while preserving the original nanoparticle size and morphology. Moreover, this preparation procedure does not require expensive experimental equipment or specialized laboratory conditions [ 64 – 65 ]. For instance, Friedfeld et al. investigated the cationic doping behavior of InP clusters with Zn²⁺ and Ga³⁺ [ 66 ]. They identified the mixed alkyl carboxylic acid cluster Zn₅(Et)₄(OAc)₆ as the most effective zinc precursor, while both Ga(OAc)₃ and [Ga(CH₃)₂(MA)]₂ exhibited comparable doping activity. Shan et al. synthesized monodisperse InP QDs with a substabilized feldspathic zincite structure through a cation exchange reaction between Cu₃P nanocrystals and In precursors in the presence of tri-n-octylphosphine [ 67 ]. By adjusting the size of Cu₃P nanocrystals, size-tunable fibrillated zincite InP QDs were obtained (as shown in Fig.  8 ), demonstrating excellent optical properties. The crystal growth process involves separating nucleation and crystal growth into two distinct steps [ 68 ]. In the first step, a homogeneous solution containing seed crystals is prepared. In the second step, the seed crystal solution is mixed with the quantum dot precursor solution at room temperature. Finally, the mixture undergoes segmented flow processing at a temperature lower than the initial seed crystal formation temperature to ensure controlled crystal growth. This approach represents a significant advancement in achieving controlled QD synthesis with a narrow size distribution. Enright et al. successfully synthesized InP nanoparticles with a particle size of 3.0 nm using this crystal growth method. Their work also demonstrated that the crystal seed growth technique can be employed to synthesize tetrahedral nanostructures, and nearly any seed crystal with an accessible (111) plane can be grown in the direction of tetrahedral prisms. This methodology not only encompasses cubic core structures but also extends to (111) planar distorted quadrilateral lattices [ 69 ].

And superior electrical properties, such as high carrier mobility with a mobility of more than 15000 cm² V − 1  S − 1 [ 71 ] , tunable energy gap (2 eV − 0.02 eV) ( [ 72 ]. And favorable biocompatibility, enable them to play an important role in the fields of efficient water treatment and pollution control, air purification and greenhouse gas control, clean energy development and energy storage, eco-friendly materials and biodegradable technology, environmental monitoring and sensor, etc. (( [ 73 – 74 ]). GQDs not only possess a series of excellent properties of graphene, but also combine the small size and quantum-limited domain effect of QDs at the same time. The height range of GQDs is usually between 0.4 and 4 nm, and the thickness is 2–4 nm, i.e., between 2-layer and 4-layer graphene sheets. The lateral dimensions are typically less than 100 nm, with most studies focusing on the range of less than 10 nm. The number of graphene layers usually consists of 1–10 layers of graphene, with most not exceeding 5 layers (( [ 75 – 76 ]). Therefore, the efficient preparation of GQDs is of great significance to the development of human life. After years of development, the preparation methods of GQDs as a whole are divided into top-down and bottom-up synthesis methods. Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs The top-down approach allows direct physical or chemical access to large-area graphene arrays into GQDs with nanometer dimensions, controlling the shape, size, and growth direction of GQDs, and is suitable for large-scale production. However, the insufficient controllability of the size and shape of QDs prepared by this method, the serious surface defects and structural damages of QDs, the low efficiency of large-scale production, the high cost and energy consumption as well as the biocompatibility of nanoparticles limit their applications in medical fields. The top-down method presents diversified technological paths in the synthesis of GQDs, such as Samra et al. used coke as a raw material (with low impurities and high carbon content) to produce GQDs by a facile process (Fig.  9 a), and spectroscopic characterization verified the feasibility [ 77 ]. Xie et al. synthesized highly crystalline monodispersed bluish N-GQDs by nitrogen-containing 3D nanocarbon electrochemical cutting (Fig.  9 b), with a QY of 19.3% and nitrogen doping of 12.3%, combining both economic and green advantages [ 78 ]. Zhou’s team innovated acid vapor cutting of bulk nitrogen-doped carbon films (1 ml of nitric acid) and in situ filtration to obtain water-soluble blue-green photoresponsive N-GQDs (1.5–3.7 nm, Fig.  10 a), circumventing the tedious isolation step [ 79 ]. Tadyszak et al. demonstrated that the that the graphene oxide precursor preparation of GOQDs did not change the C/O ratio, and found 500 nm strong fluorescence dispersion and paramagnetism under 280–380 nm excitation (Fig.  10 b) [ 80 ].  CuInS 2  QDs CuInS₂ QDs (CIS QDs) have emerged as an ideal alternative to traditional Cd/Pb-containing QDs due to their prominent advantages, including environmental benignity, low toxicity (compliant with international environmental regulations such as the EU RoHS directive), broad spectral tunability (excellent solar spectrum matching with adjustable emission ranging from 500 to 800 nm and QY up to 80%), exceptional photostability and chemical robustness (manifested in superior photobleaching resistance and stability under oxidative/acid-base environments), as well as cost-effectiveness and abundant elemental availability [ 86 – 88 ]. These distinctive characteristics render them a promising candidate for diverse applications spanning biomedical engineering, renewable energy technologies, and advanced display systems. However, the development of ternary CIS QDs still faces several challenges, including low charge injection efficiency, exciton quenching induced by interfacial space charge accumulation between charge transport layers, and interlayer miscibility during spin-coating processes [ 87 – 89 ]. Recent advancements in core-shell engineering and surface chemistry hold promise for overcoming these performance limitations, thereby accelerating the practical implementation of green nanotechnology. The following sections comprehensively review several simple yet efficient synthesis strategies for CIS QDs. Hot injection method for the Preparation of CIS QDs In the study of the synthesis of CIS QDs, hot injection is an effective means of preparing high-quality monodisperse QDs, but is limited by the scarcity of low-toxicity or nontoxic precursors. Zhu et al. applied a low-temperature hot injection preparation method to synthesize super-efficient green luminescent CIS QDs (the synthesis process appeared in Fig.  12 ). The introduction of S- Oil Amine (OAm)(S powder dissolved in ethylamine) as a sulfur precursor provided a large concentration of H 2 S at low temperature, which subsequently reacted chemically with Cu +  and In 3+ , leading to the explosive nucleation of CIS and the formation of CIS nuclei with smaller size and higher concentration [ 90 ]. Niyamakom et al. prepared ternary CIS QDs with particle sizes in the range of 7–14 nm using [Cu(acac) 2 ], [in (acac) 3 ], elemental sulfur and oleylamine (OLA) as raw materials, and investigated the effects of reaction time and precursors on the properties of the synthesized QDs. It was determined that the injection of elemental sulfur, [Cu(acac) 2 ], and oleylamine precursors in [In(acac) 3 ], respectively, initially formed a mixture of CuS nanoparticles, followed by a slow transformation to a tetragonal CIS phase (Fig.  13 ). The In content in the nanocrystals can be adjusted by changing the ratio of Cu: In precursors [ 91 ]. Liu et al. synthesized CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs using a hot injection method. Different ratios of PS-PE-BR-PS (SEBS) were used to blend with QDs to promote the dispersion of QDs, and finally a solution-based QDs/SEBS copolymer mixture was produced to form fluorescent films. The emission wavelengths and QY of CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs were 533 nm (84%) and 536 nm (97%), respectively. The emission wavelengths of CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al fluorescent films were classified as 574 nm, 582 nm, and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs fluorescent films with improved compatibility resulted in a luminescence efficiency of 51 lm/W [ 92 ]. Although the existing methods have made progress in morphology control, luminescence efficiency and dispersion improvement, they still face limitations such as high toxicity of precursors, complicated preparation process, and difficult to control the uniformity of components in large-scale production.  Cation exchange and template synthesis for the preparation of CIS QDs Cation exchange, as an efficient two-stage synthesis strategy, has become a key technology in interdisciplinary fields such as electrochemistry, chemical engineering, bioengineering, environmental protection, and optoelectronics, by preparing binary compounds of specific morphology at low temperatures and then introducing the target atoms for exchange to realize the efficient separation and purification of the target products in complex systems [ 94 ]. As applied to QDs synthesis, it can circumvent the adverse effects of high-temperature reactions, such as avoiding Ostwald ripening, preventing volatilization/decomposition of organic solvents and reducing VOCs emissions [ 95 ]. However, this method also has drawbacks, which include the susceptibility of small particles to over-exchange or compositional inhomogeneity, the susceptibility of the reaction to inverse exchange leading to compositional drift of the product, and the decrease in the fluorescence QY due to residual ionic contamination during the reaction process. Chen et al.proposed a novel low-temperature template synthesis of efficient CIS semiconductor nanocrystals by a facile cation exchange strategy using In 2 S 3  carbon nanotubes as precursors, which allowed the synthesis of a series of size-tunable CIS semiconductor nanocrystals. InP QDs Recently, InP-based QDs has become one of the hot alternatives to Cd-based QDs due to their wide spectral range, similar optoelectronic properties with Cd-based QDs, and green environmental protection, thus attracting wide attention from researchers globally. Therefore, the synthesis and application of InP-based QDs will have an extremely important potential role in the future breakthrough of quantum dot display and lighting technology. Besides, eco-friendly InP QDs do not contain restricted substances such as Cd, Pb, Hg and fulfill the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS), Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), and other regulations. The development of eco-friendly InP QDs is a combination of “compliance dividend” and “green premium”, which creates long-term value for enterprises by reducing legal risks, gaining policy support, and enhancing market competitiveness. At present, the most usual methods for the synthesis of InP QDs are as follows; Solvothermal preparation of inp QDs The solvothermal method represents an efficient and rapid approach for synthesizing highly crystalline and monodisperse InP QDs. This synthetic route involves the introduction of precursor mixtures into a solvent maintained at a specific temperature under an inert gas atmosphere, facilitating the instantaneous crystallization of InP monomers into core structures. This method offers precise control over QDs size, thereby enabling effective bandgap engineering. However, the method requires high temperature and Pressure confined system (usually > 300 °C, > 10 MPa), which increases the risk of explosion and the difficulty of safe operation. And its solvent and precursor toxicity will cause a certain burden on the environment. As demonstrated by Sarma et al., the solvothermal synthesis route successfully produced InP QDs with exceptional crystallinity and stability. These QDs exhibited small particle sizes, tunable within the range of 2.5–3.7 nm, achieved by adjusting the reaction temperature between 300 and 430 °C. This temperature modulation resulted in a bandgap tuning range of approximately 0.4 eV within the visible spectrum. The established methodology for InP QDs synthesis serves as a valuable reference for fabricating other III-V semiconductor QDs. Nozik et al. further employed the solvothermal method to synthesize InP QDs with an average particle size of 2.5 ± 0.19 nm [ 51 ]. Yang et al. advanced this technique by developing a stepwise solvothermal approach to synthesize highly fluorescent InP/ZnS core-shell QDs, achieving a remarkable fluorescence QY of 41–42%. Notably, the use of P(N(CH₃)₂)₃ as a precursor offers significant advantages over P(TMS)₃, being both less toxic and more cost-effective, aligning with the principles of green chemistry and sustainable material synthesis [ 52 ]. Kuo et al.further demonstrated the potential of this approach by utilizing safe, eco-friendly, and low-cost precursors to synthesize InP/ZnS core-shell QDs with tunable fluorescence properties through the green solvothermal method, achieving an impressive fluorescence QY of 60.1% [ 53 ].Thus, the solvothermal method shows potential in the controlled synthesis and green improvement of InP QDs, but its harsh synthesis conditions, inherent defect control problems and scale-up barriers are still the core barriers to industrialization. In the future, synergistic breakthroughs in performance and sustainability should be realized through reaction path innovation, precise structure regulation and green process iteration. Heating method for the preparation of inp QDs The heating method is a reliable and scalable technique for colloidal nanocrystal synthesis, which enables controlled nucleation and crystal growth by dissolving precursors and ligands in solvents and initiating reactions by heating. By optimizing the precursors, stabilizers and heating rate, high quality nanocrystals comparable to thermal injection can be produced. However, the decomposition of ligands (e.g., oleylamine) at high temperatures releases amine gases that irritate the respiratory tract. These gases participate in photochemical reactions to form secondary pollutants such as ozone. Rapid nucleation is also prone to causing lattice distortion and high defect densities in QDs. To mitigate environmental impact, solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine) can be recovered via distillation or adsorption techniques, enabling closed-loop production. Figure  4 a illustrates the fundamental process of nanocrystal formation in heated synthesis and its correlation with the reaction vessel temperature [ 54 ]. Pidluzhna et al. employed the heating method to prepare core-shell InP/ZnS hybrid QDs, as depicted in Fig.  4 b Their study focused on the applicability of these synthesized InP/ZnS core-shell QDs in the stepwise fabrication of inverted solar cells, utilizing a combination of thermal vacuum deposition and spin-coating techniques [ 55 ]. Wang et al. developed cadmium-free InP/ZnSeS/ZnS thick-shell QDs using the heating method. By varying the number of zinc sources, they controlled the emission wavelength of the InP core and optimized the thickness of the ZnS layer, thereby enhancing the quality of the QDs [ 56 ]. Kim et al. reported a simple one-pot heating method for synthesizing InP and InP/ZnS core-shell QDs. By precisely controlling the flow rate and crystal growth temperature, they successfully synthesized high-quality InP/ZnS QDs with tunable emission wavelengths ranging from blue-green to red [ 57 ].Summarizing, the heating method in the synthesis of InP-based QDs exhibits the advantages of controllable core-shell structure construction, precise emission wavelength tuning, and highly efficient synthesis in a one-pot method. However, the limitations such as unresolved environmental risks, insufficient defects control, and poor process scalability are generally present. In the future, further breakthroughs can be achieved by developing bio-based ligands to replace oleylamine and coupling distillation/adsorption to achieve closed-loop production, introducing gradient shell layers and post-processing passivation to reduce the defect density, as well as combining microfluidic continuous-flow synthesis with machine-learning optimization of parameters.

 Hot injection method for the preparation of inp QDs The hot-injection method achieves the separation of nucleation and growth phases by dissolving the precursor in organic solvents (e.g., octadecene, oleylamine, and trioctylphosphine) by heating and injecting another precursor several times at a specific temperature to trigger the transient supersaturation of the solution, which allows for the homogeneous nucleation and controlled growth of crystals, and the products are both monodispersed and homogeneous; the variety of the choice of the reaction solvents and active agents further expand the product system [ 34 – 58 ]. However, the volatilization/decomposition of solvents at high temperatures (> 300 °C) releases volatile organic compounds (VOCs) (amines, alkanes, etc.), which causes air pollution and health risks, and requires secondary treatment of the exhaust gases and waste liquids. For example, Jamshidi Zavaraki et al. employed a hot injection method to synthesize colloidal InP and ZnS-covered InP QDs, which were successfully applied for the first time as sensitizers in quantum dot-sensitized solar cells (QDSSCs) [ 59 ]. However, the stability of colloidal InP QDs was lower and the sensitivity to moisture is higher, so ZnS coating was used in this work to enhance the stability of InP and to protect InP QDs from moisture and interaction with electrolytes. Song et al. first introduced of high-quality InP QDs by the reaction of P(N(CH 3 ) 2 ) 3  hot injected at 220 °C with In and Zn chlorides dissolved in the relatively weakly coordinated solvent oleylamine, and achieved an unprecedented series of controlled synthesis of bandgap-tunable InP QDs, successfully achieving nucleation/growth of QDs (Fig.  5 ) [ 60 ]. Ramasamy et al. prepared InP/ZnS core-shell QDs using the hot injection method, and in this experiment, it was found that the presence of a small amount of water as an impurity not only significantly reduced the FWHM and increased the QY of InP/ZnS QDs [ 61 ]. InP/ZnS QDs obtained using In precursors and the presence of water in the solvent had a narrow FWHM of 46 nm and a high QY of 45%. In comparison, without water doping, the emission wavelength of the synthesized QDs was around 625 nm, with a FWHM of 66 nm and a QY of about 33% (its High Resolution Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) schematic of QDs synthesized with and without water was displayed in Fig.  6 ). Singh et al. successfully synthesized InP QDs and InP/ZnS core-shell structures using the hot injection technique. It was observed that the PL intensity increased gradually when the ZnS shell layer was increased, and the synthesized QDs were treated with HF to remove the defects on the surface of QDs and thus enhanced the luminescence intensity [ 62 ]. Hot injection method shows multiple breakthroughs in the synthesis of InP QDs. However, the method still suffers from limitations such as high-temperature decomposition of solvents, unidentified mechanism of water impurity enhancement, and strong corrosive waste liquid from strong acid treatment. In the future, we need to focus on the development of low-toxicity solvents to replace oleylamine, establish a quantitative model of water content and defect states to stabilize the process, and explore green defect passivation techniques such as photo/thermal annealing.

 In addition to the aforementioned common preparation methods, alternative approaches such as ion exchange and crystal growth techniques, have been developed. The ion exchange system (Fig.  7 ) addresses the limitations of conventional crystal preparation methods and has emerged as a superior alternative for fabricating semiconductor nanostructures with phases that are challenging to obtain through direct chemical synthesis [ 63 ]. In this method, guest ions in organic or aqueous solvents replace cations in the host material, facilitating rapid ion exchange among Group II-VI, I-VI, and IV-VI semiconductors while preserving the original nanoparticle size and morphology. Moreover, this preparation procedure does not require expensive experimental equipment or specialized laboratory conditions [ 64 – 65 ]. For instance, Friedfeld et al. investigated the cationic doping behavior of InP clusters with Zn²⁺ and Ga³⁺ [ 66 ]. They identified the mixed alkyl carboxylic acid cluster Zn₅(Et)₄(OAc)₆ as the most effective zinc precursor, while both Ga(OAc)₃ and [Ga(CH₃)₂(MA)]₂ exhibited comparable doping activity. Shan et al. synthesized monodisperse InP QDs with a substabilized feldspathic zincite structure through a cation exchange reaction between Cu₃P nanocrystals and In precursors in the presence of tri-n-octylphosphine [ 67 ]. By adjusting the size of Cu₃P nanocrystals, size-tunable fibrillated zincite InP QDs were obtained (as shown in Fig.  8 ), demonstrating excellent optical properties. The crystal growth process involves separating nucleation and crystal growth into two distinct steps [ 68 ]. In the first step, a homogeneous solution containing seed crystals is prepared. In the second step, the seed crystal solution is mixed with the quantum dot precursor solution at room temperature. Finally, the mixture undergoes segmented flow processing at a temperature lower than the initial seed crystal formation temperature to ensure controlled crystal growth. This approach represents a significant advancement in achieving controlled QD synthesis with a narrow size distribution. Enright et al. successfully synthesized InP nanoparticles with a particle size of 3.0 nm using this crystal growth method. Their work also demonstrated that the crystal seed growth technique can be employed to synthesize tetrahedral nanostructures, and nearly any seed crystal with an accessible (111) plane can be grown in the direction of tetrahedral prisms. This methodology not only encompasses cubic core structures but also extends to (111) planar distorted quadrilateral lattices [ 69 ].

The ion exchange system (Fig.  7 ) addresses the limitations of conventional crystal preparation methods and has emerged as a superior alternative for fabricating semiconductor nanostructures with phases that are challenging to obtain through direct chemical synthesis [ 63 ]. In this method, guest ions in organic or aqueous solvents replace cations in the host material, facilitating rapid ion exchange among Group II-VI, I-VI, and IV-VI semiconductors while preserving the original nanoparticle size and morphology. Graphene QDs As an emerging eco-friendly nanomaterial, GQDs, with their unique physicochemical properties, such as high specific surface area (300–600 m 2 /g), excellent optical properties, such as strong fluorescence properties, tunable fluorescence, and high optical absorption from UV to IR ( [ 70 ]. And superior electrical properties, such as high carrier mobility with a mobility of more than 15000 cm² V − 1  S − 1 [ 71 ] , tunable energy gap (2 eV − 0.02 eV) ( [ 72 ]. And favorable biocompatibility, enable them to play an important role in the fields of efficient water treatment and pollution control, air purification and greenhouse gas control, clean energy development and energy storage, eco-friendly materials and biodegradable technology, environmental monitoring and sensor, etc. (( [ 73 – 74 ]). GQDs not only possess a series of excellent properties of graphene, but also combine the small size and quantum-limited domain effect of QDs at the same time. The height range of GQDs is usually between 0.4 and 4 nm, and the thickness is 2–4 nm, i.e., between 2-layer and 4-layer graphene sheets. The lateral dimensions are typically less than 100 nm, with most studies focusing on the range of less than 10 nm. The number of graphene layers usually consists of 1–10 layers of graphene, with most not exceeding 5 layers (( [ 75 – 76 ]). Therefore, the efficient preparation of GQDs is of great significance to the development of human life. After years of development, the preparation methods of GQDs as a whole are divided into top-down and bottom-up synthesis methods. Top-down method for the preparation of GQDs The top-down approach allows direct physical or chemical access to large-area graphene arrays into GQDs with nanometer dimensions, controlling the shape, size, and growth direction of GQDs, and is suitable for large-scale production. However, the insufficient controllability of the size and shape of QDs prepared by this method, the serious surface defects and structural damages of QDs, the low efficiency of large-scale production, the high cost and energy consumption as well as the biocompatibility of nanoparticles limit their applications in medical fields. The top-down method presents diversified technological paths in the synthesis of GQDs, such as Samra et al. used coke as a raw material (with low impurities and high carbon content) to produce GQDs by a facile process (Fig.  9 a), and spectroscopic characterization verified the feasibility [ 77 ]. Xie et al. synthesized highly crystalline monodispersed bluish N-GQDs by nitrogen-containing 3D nanocarbon electrochemical cutting (Fig.  9 b), with a QY of 19.3% and nitrogen doping of 12.3%, combining both economic and green advantages [ 78 ]. Zhou’s team innovated acid vapor cutting of bulk nitrogen-doped carbon films (1 ml of nitric acid) and in situ filtration to obtain water-soluble blue-green photoresponsive N-GQDs (1.5–3.7 nm, Fig.  10 a), circumventing the tedious isolation step [ 79 ]. Tadyszak et al. demonstrated that the that the graphene oxide precursor preparation of GOQDs did not change the C/O ratio, and found 500 nm strong fluorescence dispersion and paramagnetism under 280–380 nm excitation (Fig.  10 b) [ 80 ]. Soriano et al. developed GQDs fluorescence for the detection of carbamates in water by using mixed-acid oxidation to modulate the reaction time (Fig.  10 c) [ 81 ].However, there are core limitations of this method, such as the strong corrosive waste liquid generated by the acid treatment method, the still low QY (< 20%) and the unclear mechanism of magnetic/optical property regulation. In the future, it could be attempted to develop green stripping technologies like laser/plasma to replace the strong acid process, construct doping-fluorescence-magnetism constitutive relationship models, and explore biomass carbon sources to reduce costs and increase efficiency.

The advantage of this method is that it is easy to control the shape and size of GQDs, which is an irreplaceable advantage in regulating the physical properties and molecular structure of substances. Prof. Chiang’s team investigated a bottom-up preparation method for the synthesis of colloidal QDs using an aqueous organosulfate solution treated with an atmospheric pressure argon (Ar) microplasma [ 83 ]. The average diameter of the fabricated colloidal GQDs was 4.9 nm, the QY was 1.5%, and the room temperature photoluminescence peak was 448 nm. Xu et al.used a top-down preparation method to synthesize GQDs with high solubility and excellent film-forming ability in common organic solvents. Significantly, this research not only solved the limitation of low solubility of GQDs prepared by traditional methods in organic solubility but also expected to successfully apply GQDs in other optoelectronic fields [ 84 ].Gao’s team applied a bottom-up synthesis method to prepare two water-soluble GQDs with different degrees of oxidation using graphene molecules, namely O-GQDs prepared by oxidation and R-QDs synthesized by reduction. Although the bottom-up method is novel and green, the current quantum efficiency is low; the top-down method is effective in solving the solubility problem, but has deficiencies in the complexity of the preparation process, etc. In the future, it is expected to optimize the preparation method to improve the quantum efficiency and further expand the applications in the field of optoelectronics.
