CuInS 2  QDs CuInS₂ QDs (CIS QDs) have emerged as an ideal alternative to traditional Cd/Pb-containing QDs due to their prominent advantages, including environmental benignity, low toxicity (compliant with international environmental regulations such as the EU RoHS directive), broad spectral tunability (excellent solar spectrum matching with adjustable emission ranging from 500 to 800 nm and QY up to 80%), exceptional photostability and chemical robustness (manifested in superior photobleaching resistance and stability under oxidative/acid-base environments), as well as cost-effectiveness and abundant elemental availability [ 86 – 88 ]. These distinctive characteristics render them a promising candidate for diverse applications spanning biomedical engineering, renewable energy technologies, and advanced display systems. However, the development of ternary CIS QDs still faces several challenges, including low charge injection efficiency, exciton quenching induced by interfacial space charge accumulation between charge transport layers, and interlayer miscibility during spin-coating processes [ 87 – 89 ]. Recent advancements in core-shell engineering and surface chemistry hold promise for overcoming these performance limitations, thereby accelerating the practical implementation of green nanotechnology. The following sections comprehensively review several simple yet efficient synthesis strategies for CIS QDs. Hot injection method for the Preparation of CIS QDs In the study of the synthesis of CIS QDs, hot injection is an effective means of preparing high-quality monodisperse QDs, but is limited by the scarcity of low-toxicity or nontoxic precursors. Zhu et al. applied a low-temperature hot injection preparation method to synthesize super-efficient green luminescent CIS QDs (the synthesis process appeared in Fig.  12 ). The introduction of S- Oil Amine (OAm)(S powder dissolved in ethylamine) as a sulfur precursor provided a large concentration of H 2 S at low temperature, which subsequently reacted chemically with Cu +  and In 3+ , leading to the explosive nucleation of CIS and the formation of CIS nuclei with smaller size and higher concentration [ 90 ]. Niyamakom et al. prepared ternary CIS QDs with particle sizes in the range of 7–14 nm using [Cu(acac) 2 ], [in (acac) 3 ], elemental sulfur and oleylamine (OLA) as raw materials, and investigated the effects of reaction time and precursors on the properties of the synthesized QDs. It was determined that the injection of elemental sulfur, [Cu(acac) 2 ], and oleylamine precursors in [In(acac) 3 ], respectively, initially formed a mixture of CuS nanoparticles, followed by a slow transformation to a tetragonal CIS phase (Fig.  13 ). The In content in the nanocrystals can be adjusted by changing the ratio of Cu: In precursors [ 91 ]. Liu et al. synthesized CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs using a hot injection method. Different ratios of PS-PE-BR-PS (SEBS) were used to blend with QDs to promote the dispersion of QDs, and finally a solution-based QDs/SEBS copolymer mixture was produced to form fluorescent films. The emission wavelengths and QY of CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs were 533 nm (84%) and 536 nm (97%), respectively. The emission wavelengths of CIS/ZnS and CIS/ZnS: Al fluorescent films were classified as 574 nm, 582 nm, and CIS/ZnS: Al QDs fluorescent films with improved compatibility resulted in a luminescence efficiency of 51 lm/W [ 92 ]. Bao et al. fabricated monodisperse CIS nanocrystals by injecting mixed metal oleic acid (OA) precursors into hot organic solvents containing dissolved sulfur sources, such as OLA, 1-octadecene (ODE), OA, and their mixtures with dissolved sulfur sources. Different shapes of CIS nanocrystals were synthesized by changing the preparation conditions, such as triangular pyramids with tunable crystalline phases, bullet-like rods and conical anisotropic crystals [ 93 ]. Although the existing methods have made progress in morphology control, luminescence efficiency and dispersion improvement, they still face limitations such as high toxicity of precursors, complicated preparation process, and difficult to control the uniformity of components in large-scale production. Future research could focus on the development of environment-friendly precursors, optimization of the hot injection process to simplify the process and improve the reproducibility of production.

 Cation exchange and template synthesis for the preparation of CIS QDs Cation exchange, as an efficient two-stage synthesis strategy, has become a key technology in interdisciplinary fields such as electrochemistry, chemical engineering, bioengineering, environmental protection, and optoelectronics, by preparing binary compounds of specific morphology at low temperatures and then introducing the target atoms for exchange to realize the efficient separation and purification of the target products in complex systems [ 94 ]. As applied to QDs synthesis, it can circumvent the adverse effects of high-temperature reactions, such as avoiding Ostwald ripening, preventing volatilization/decomposition of organic solvents and reducing VOCs emissions [ 95 ]. However, this method also has drawbacks, which include the susceptibility of small particles to over-exchange or compositional inhomogeneity, the susceptibility of the reaction to inverse exchange leading to compositional drift of the product, and the decrease in the fluorescence QY due to residual ionic contamination during the reaction process. Chen et al.proposed a novel low-temperature template synthesis of efficient CIS semiconductor nanocrystals by a facile cation exchange strategy using In 2 S 3  carbon nanotubes as precursors, which allowed the synthesis of a series of size-tunable CIS semiconductor nanocrystals. By reasonably controlling the Cu/In stoichiometry, the efficient luminescence of CIS with a maximum QY of 28.6% was obtained [ 96 ]. Xia et al. reported a multi-step seeded growth synthesis of CuInS₂/ZnS core/rod-shell QDs, wherein wurtzite CuInS₂ NCs were obtained through localized Cu⁺and In³⁺ cation exchange within template Cu₂₋ₓS NCs (synthetic steps illustrated in Fig.  14 a). The resulting colloidal wurtzite CuInS₂/ZnS core/rod-shell QDs exhibited a high molar extinction coefficient, near-infrared PL with QY of 20%, and excellent dispersibility in diverse solvents [ 97 ]. Thiel et al. investigated the formation of fibrillated zincite CIS NCs from copper-deficient djurleite Cu 2 -xS nanorods using a cation exchange method. A wide temperature range of 40 °C to 160 °C allows for a variety of intermediates to be realized while retaining size and shape., synthesis schematic as in Fig.  14 b [ 98 ].These methods have their own characteristics in the preparation process and performance, and although progress has been made in QY, size regulation, optical properties, etc., there exist limitations such as relatively cumbersome process steps, difficulty in controlling the cation exchange process, harsh conditions in some syntheses, and difficulty in large-scale production [ 38 ,  99 ,  100 ]. In the future, efforts can be made to simplify the synthesis process, optimize the parameters of the cation exchange process to improve reproducibility, and explore milder and easier-to-control synthesis conditions (Table  2 ).

Eco-friendly QDs in different fields from an environmental compliance perspective From the perspective of environmental compliance, eco-friendly QDs exhibit significant advantages in different applications. In the display and lighting fields, they do not contain heavy metals such as Pb, Cd, etc., which are subject to regulatory restrictions, and fulfill the requirements of the EU RoHS and REACH regulations on the limits of hazardous substances in electronic devices, avoiding the risk of soil/water contamination caused by the leakage of heavy metals in traditional Cd-based QDs, and at the same time reducing volatile organic emissions in the production process through the solution method printing process. In the field of sensing, low-toxicity materials represented by GQDs comply with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) specification on the biocompatibility of nanomaterials, and its near-infrared luminescent properties can reduce the use of chemical stains in in vivo imaging and circumvent the bioaccumulative toxicity of traditional fluorescent dyes. In the field of energy and environment, heavy metal-free QDs can be used in solar cells through a simple recycling process, complying with the requirements of the EU’s New Battery Law on the recycling rate of battery components, and its photocatalytic degradation of pollutants does not produce secondary heavy metal pollution, conforming to the environmental protection standards of China’s Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution for the treatment of industrial wastewater. Applications of inp QDs in different fields InP QDs for solar cell applications As a central pillar of the transition from a carbon-based civilization to a photonic civilization, solar cell technology directly addresses environmental challenges through zero-emission operation and resource sustainability, synergizes global emissions reduction policies, and drives innovation in the economic model, enhanced social equity, and restructuring of global governance, Its continued breakthroughs will support the carbon neutrality goal and the development of the circular economy, laying the core cornerstone of ecological civilization construction. So far, III-V group semiconductors have been the benchmark materials for solar energy conversion devices. Among them, as a representative III-V compound, InP (indium phosphide) has excellent radiation resistance, high photoelectric conversion efficiency, ideal bandgap characteristics, and environmental friendliness, and can be widely used in space exploration, aerospace, and terrestrial concentrating systems. Furthermore, InP-based solar cells simultaneously achieve high efficiency (up to 23.6% in single-junction configurations) and chemical stability, while their radiation tolerance (10⁶ rad(Si)) is two orders of magnitude greater than that of silicon and one order of magnitude superior to that of GaAs. These attributes endow InP solar cells with unmatched potential for advanced energy harvesting scenarios requiring both performance and reliability [ 101 – 103 ]. Gupta et al. achieved 19.3% efficient p-InP solar cells using TiO2 as an ESC layer and hydrogen plasma treatment (Fig.  15 ), which reduced bulk carrier concentration via near-surface charge inversion, offering insights for efficient optoelectronic device fabrication [ 104 ]. Crisp et al. prepared InP/InZnP quantum dot solar cells (QDSCs, Fig.  16 ) with photoelectric conversion efficiencies of 0.65% and 1.2%, respectively. The study shows that carrier transport in InP QDs films is dominated by trap effects, while zinc doping can suppress traps and enhance photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). After ligand exchange with (NH₄)₂S solution, the carrier mobility and lifetime reach the level of PbS QDs, marking a major breakthrough in the development of cadmium-free and lead-free green optoelectronic devices [ 105 ]. Moreover, Jing et al. fabricated a “giant” InP/ZnSe QDs light-emitting solar concentrator (LSC) based on tapered InP/ZnSe QDs with different ZnSe shell thicknesses, and achieved an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 2.5% and a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 2.0% under simulated sunlight. This class-leading performance demonstrates the potential of environmentally friendly LSC technology [ 106 ]. Goldman et al. demonstrated that InP solar cells coated with TiO 2  nanopillar arrays achieve sub-wavelength optical engineering through synergistic Mie scattering resonance and thin-film interference effects, reducing reflectivity to less than 1% in the 800–1200 nm wavelength band while maintaining the electronic integrity of the InP absorber layer. The structure avoids the need for complex multilayer dielectric films and performs comparably to top-quality quarter-wave coatings. Optical simulations indicate that its hybrid scattering-interference mechanism enhances light absorption through optical waveguide effects and diffuse scattering, and a combined photovoltaic model predicts a PCE of more than 23% at AM1.5G illumination [ 107 ]. In summary, InP QDs have made significant advancements in photovoltaics. However, limitations persist, such as the relatively low efficiency of QDSCs based on InP QDs, the insufficient light harvesting capacity of LSC, and the lack of long-term stability assessments across all studies, coupled with cost barriers to scalability. Therefore, future research should focus on enhancing QDSCs efficiency through atomic-level passivation of core-shell interfaces, constructing multifunctional nanostructures with opto-electronic synergy, and advancing accelerated aging standards alongside green manufacturing processes-aiming to drive breakthroughs in III-V photovoltaics and QDs technologies towards high-efficiency, stability, and environmental sustainability.

While current InP QDs-based red/green QLEDs achieve efficiencies (EQE of 21.4%) rivaling state-of-the-art Cd-based devices, with solution fluorescence QYs approaching 100%, blue-emitting devices suffer from severely lagging efficiency due to high trap-state density caused by lattice mismatch between small-sized InP cores and shell materials. Breaking this blue-light bottleneck represents a critical milestone to accelerate the development of the full InP QLEDs field. It will further establish this technology as an interdisciplinary paradigm integrating materials science, environmental policy, and industrial strategy, propelling the sustainable transformation of the display industry [ 108 – 110 ]. For example, Yang et al. synthesized blue-emitting InP/ZnS/ZnS QDs with a PL peak at 465 nm, FWHM of 38 nm, and PLQY of 96% using a two-step heating and thick-shell strategy. Leveraging these QDs, they fabricated high-efficiency inkjet-printed blue InP QLEDs. Despite the exceptional QDs performance, blue InP QLEDs efficiency remains significantly lower than red/green counterparts due to high trap densities arising from the substantial lattice mismatch between small-sized InP cores and shell materials. By employing dual zinc precursors to control graded shell growth and suppress energy transfer, the team produced high-PLQY QDs films—marking a critical milestone for advancing large-area full-color electroluminescent displays. Overcoming this bottleneck is essential to accelerate progress across the entire InP QLEDs field [ 111 ].Additionally, Zhao et al. synthesized narrow-band InP/ZnSeS/ZnS QDs via a facile one-pot method, utilizing safe tris(dimethylamino)phosphine as the phosphorus precursor. The ZnSeS inner shell was formed through solution growth under a temperature gradient of 240–280 °C, with growth dynamics and PL intensity characterized as shown in Fig.  17 . The resulting InP/ZnSeS/ZnS QDs exhibited a PLQY of 91% and a FWHM of 36 nm. Finally, QLEDs fabricated with these QDs demonstrated a narrow emission bandwidth of 42 nm, representing the smallest reported emission width for green InP QLEDs using safe phosphorus precursors to date [ 112 ]. Long et al. synthesized highly efficient InP/ZnSe/ZnSeS/ZnS QDs with a FWHM of 41 nm and a PLQY of ~ 96%. QLEDs based on these InP QDs not only achieved high brightness but also demonstrated an EQE of 12.39% (as shown in Fig.  18 ). This work laid a technical foundation for the development of high-quality and eco-friendly InP-based QDs [ 113 ]. Future efforts must focus on: developing lattice-mismatch compensation techniques to boost blue-light efficiency, optimizing synthesis routes for safe precursors to rival toxic counterparts, establishing accelerated aging standards for QLEDs devices, and advancing the industrial commercialization of cadmium-free quantum dot display technologies.

This breakthrough enabled QDs to serve as fluorescent labels for bioimaging and biodetection, marking the first biomedically relevant application of QDs. Since then, QDs has emerged as promising candidates for multiplexed bioassays and chemical sensing platforms due to their narrow emission bandwidths and resistance to photobleaching [ 115 ]. Among them, InP QDs has found particular utility in biofluorescence imaging and in vivo cellular tracking because of their intrinsic biocompatibility, robust core-shell architectures, and low cytotoxicity compared to cadmium-based counterparts [ 116 ]. These attributes make InP QDs ideal for long-term in vitro diagnostics and deep-tissue imaging, where material stability and safety are critical. Yang et al. developed an InP/ZnS quantum dot-based fluorescent probe for highly sensitive and selective detection of horseradish peroxidase (HRP) via a static fluorescence quenching mechanism, where HRP and QDs form a ground-state complex. This complex reduces HRP’s α-helical content and diminishes its thermal stability. After systematic optimization of parameters—including quantum dot concentration, pH, and ionic strength—the probe achieved a linear detection range of 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ to 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ M (corresponding to enzymatic activity of 0.01–0.3 U/mL) with a detection limit as low as 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ M (1.2 mU/mL) (as for Fig.  19 ). In an electrolytic environment simulating electric field changes across cell membranes, they discovered that Group II-VI (CdSe/CdS) and III-V (InP/ZnS) QDs respond to ionic gradient-induced electric fields (with ionic screening lengths spanning 0.3 nm to 300 nm). Their PL demonstrated 50% greater sensitivity to AC/DC voltage fluctuations than state-of-the-art calcium indicators. This device provides critical technical support for developing reproducible QD-based voltage sensors and confirms the potential of InP/ZnS QDs for dynamic voltage tracking in living cells [ 118 ]. And Zhang et al. developed a fluorescent visualization sensor based on MPA-coated InP/ZnS QDs and sodium rhodizonate (SR) for sensitive monitoring of fish freshness. The sensor’s performance—including sensitivity, interference resistance, stability, and reversibility—was assessed through NH₃gas-sensing tests, demonstrating a detection limit of 3 ppm for volatile amine gases.  GQD for sensing applications GQDs has significant advantages in sensor applications: its excellent optical properties (strong fluorescence, broad excitation spectrum, stability) enable high-sensitivity fluorescence sensing. The large specific surface area and rich surface functional groups provide sufficient binding sites for enhanced selectivity and loading, especially for biomolecule trapping. Excellent electrical properties (high mobility, conductivity) can accelerate electron transfer and enhance the response speed and accuracy of electrochemical sensors. Good biocompatibility and low toxicity make them suitable for biomedical sensing such as cell imaging and in vivo detection. In addition, their relatively simple preparation process, low cost, and adjustable structure (size, functional groups) facilitate scale-up production and customized sensor design for specific needs, enhancing flexibility and versatility [ 131 – 134 ]. Morsy’s team successfully prepared g-C 3 N 4 /GQDs nanocomposites and developed humidity sensors. The composite QDs were characterized by various techniques, which confirmed that the composite QDs has suitable particle size, good morphology and high structure-chemistry matching. GQDs also have great potential for application in optical sensing, such as Raeyani’s team developed a room-temperature GQDs optical CO 2  sensor (the reaction-recovery curves upon exposure to carbon dioxide are shown in Fig.  24 ), whose optical absorption characteristics showed significant sensitivity to CO 2  concentration changes [ 136 ].Shehab et al. prepared a phenylboronic acid-functionalized GQDs fluorescent sensor, which can achieve easy and stable detection of human serum glucose [ 137 ].Liu’s team constructed a boron-doped GQDs fluorescent sensor array, which can achieve broad linear detection of six plasticizers (100 ng/mL-195 mg/mL) with ng detection limit and 95–106% recovery by analyzing the fluorescent signal changes caused by plasticizers (dispersive and electron transfer effects), and has highly reproducible, stable, and reproducible results. The results demonstrated that the method is highly reproducible, specific and practical [ 138 ]. However, there are still some challenges in GQDs sensor research: (1) Most of the work focuses on laboratory environment validation and lacks universal testing in complex real-world scenarios. (2) Insufficient analysis of sensing mechanisms, etc. Therefore, the future can be carried out in the following aspects: (1) technology expansion - optical properties and electrical performance synergies can be developed multi-modal sensors to enhance the detection dimension. (2) Application deepening-functionalized design can be customized with high specificity probes to promote in vivo diagnosis and food safety.

 Applications of CIS QDs in different fields CIS QDs for solar cells applications CIS-based QDs offer significant advantages in solar cells: their 1.5–1.8 eV energy band structure matches the solar spectrum for efficient capture of visible-near-infrared light. Excellent carrier transport properties promote rapid photogenerated charge separation, enhancing short-circuit current and fill factor. Environmental friendliness (heavy metal free) and low-cost solution method preparation (spin coating/inkjet printing) support scale-up production. Fine tuning of size, composition, and surface ligands optimizes the energy level matching of optoelectronic devices, simultaneously enhancing performance and long-term operational reliability [ 139 – 140 ]. As a representative study, Several teams have enhanced the performance of CIS QDs solar cells through interface engineering. For example, Konstantatos et al. used formic acid ligand exchange to construct a non-annealed CIS photoconductive film in a TiO 2  porous network, and optimized the thickness of the absorber layer and carrier mobility to improve the PCE by a 7.7-fold factor, from 0.05–1.16%.The performance evolution was quantitatively verified through J-V characterization, with the corresponding curves and detailed photovoltaic parameters documented in Fig.  25  [ 141 ]。Gao et al. design TiO 2 -CIS nanorod arrays to achieve the highest efficiency of 11.7% by utilizing CIS to enhance the light trapping and electron injection capabilities [ 142 ]. Peng et al. modulated the TiO 2 /CIS photoelectrode interfacial contact by heat treatment (300℃ optimum) to promote charge separation and transfer, and PCE was improved from 4.04 to 4.68%. The photoelectric properties are characterized as shown in Fig.  26  [ 143 ].Wang et al. prepared solar cells based on CIS QDs using anatase TiO 2  nanodendrite arrays instead of nanowires, and the results showed that the CIS QDSCs were able to achieve higher current density and increase PCE from 4.7 to 5.48%, and that their photovoltaic electrodes exhibited excellent charge generation and charge separation capabilities [ 144 ]. Current research on QDSCs based on CIS QDs is still limited by (1) low absolute efficiency and enhancement dependence on specific structures. (2) High process complexity, which restricts the large-scale production. (3) The interface regulation mechanism is not fully elucidated. Therefore, in the future, the bottleneck can be broken through (1) energy band engineering to synergistically optimize light trapping and charge transport. (2) Process innovation to develop low-temperature/no annealing technology.

Applications of GQDs in different fields GQD for solar cell applications Graphene, leveraging its exceptional optoelectronic properties, biological safety, and processability advantages, has emerged as a research hotspot in the nanomaterials field. It demonstrates irreplaceable application value across disciplines such as biomedicine, optoelectronic sensing, photovoltaic energy, and environmental science [ 120 – 121 ]. Over the years, continuous exploration of graphene-based materials has revealed significant potential for enhancing solar cell performance through graphene-derived nanocrystals [ 122 – 123 ]. GQDs has achieved triple breakthroughs in photovoltaics: First, Ding’s team enhanced cathode interlayer performance in polymer solar cells via edge-tetramethylammonium functionalization (GQD-TMA), achieving PCEs of 7.01% for PCDTBT: PC₇₁BM and 8.80% for PTB7-Th: PC₇₁BM systems—significantly outperforming conventional Ca/LiF/ZnO interlayers (< 6.5%) (compare J-V plots as displayed in Fig.  21 ). Second, Wang introduced GQDs into molybdenum disulfide/indium phosphide (MoS₂/InP) van der Waals heterostructures, where photo-induced doping modulated the potential barrier height, boosting device PCE from 2.1 to 4.1%. Finally, Lin employed pulsed laser ablation to synthesize 3.8 nm GQDs, which enhanced short-circuit current, fill factor, and PCE in InGaP/InGaAs/Ge triple-junction solar cells through carrier injection, with mechanisms validated by transient PL, EQE, and Kelvin probe measurements [ 124 – 126 ]. GQDs photovoltaic applications remain constrained by: (1) solution-processing limitations hindering large-area fabrication, (2) inadequately suppressed charge recombination at heterojunction interfaces, and (3) lack of long-term photothermal stability studies. Future efforts should prioritize developing solid-state GQDs dispersion techniques for roll-to-roll manufacturing and designing graded energy-level alignment interlayers to minimize heterojunction potential barrier losses.

(4) Environmentally friendly, no heavy metal components and excellent biocompatibility, complying with international environmental standards such as the EU ErP Directive. Li’s team developed an ultrafast microwave synthesis method to prepare single-crystalline layered MA-GQDs, achieving a fluorescence quantum efficiency of 35% (with absorption extending to 700 nm; PLQY under different conditions shown in Fig.  22 ). These were successfully applied as phosphorescent probes for white QLEDs and cellular imaging. Lee et al. pioneered controllable-size synthesis of hexagonal single-crystal GQDs, revealing the edge-state regulation mechanism of exciton lifetimes, while also preparing 2D/3D graphene single crystals from D-glucose. Son et al. employed graphene-ZnO core-shell structures to fabricate white QLEDs with a luminance of 798 cd/m², demonstrating GQDs’ versatility in luminescent devices [ 128 – 130 ]. GQD-based QLEDs still face limitations including low quantum efficiency, insufficient industrial-grade luminance, and inadequate bending stability in flexible devices. Future breakthroughs should focus on developing plasmon resonance energy transfer strategies to enhance exciton utilization efficiency and constructing Perovskite/GQD heterostructures to overcome brightness bottlenecks-ultimately advancing the industrialization of green ultrathin-flexible lighting technology.

The large specific surface area and rich surface functional groups provide sufficient binding sites for enhanced selectivity and loading, especially for biomolecule trapping. Excellent electrical properties (high mobility, conductivity) can accelerate electron transfer and enhance the response speed and accuracy of electrochemical sensors. Good biocompatibility and low toxicity make them suitable for biomedical sensing such as cell imaging and in vivo detection. In addition, their relatively simple preparation process, low cost, and adjustable structure (size, functional groups) facilitate scale-up production and customized sensor design for specific needs, enhancing flexibility and versatility [ 131 – 134 ]. Morsy’s team successfully prepared g-C 3 N 4 /GQDs nanocomposites and developed humidity sensors. As shown in Fig.  23 , the tests at a wide humidity range of 7%-97% and multiple frequencies indicate that the sensor has the advantages of excellent reversibility, fast response/recovery speed, strong anti-interference, low cost, and ease of use, which is promising for the applications in the fields of humidity alarms and respiratory analysis [ 135 ]. GQDs also have great potential for application in optical sensing, such as Raeyani’s team developed a room-temperature GQDs optical CO 2  sensor (the reaction-recovery curves upon exposure to carbon dioxide are shown in Fig.  24 ), whose optical absorption characteristics showed significant sensitivity to CO 2  concentration changes [ 136 ].Shehab et al. prepared a phenylboronic acid-functionalized GQDs fluorescent sensor, which can achieve easy and stable detection of human serum glucose [ 137 ].Liu’s team constructed a boron-doped GQDs fluorescent sensor array, which can achieve broad linear detection of six plasticizers (100 ng/mL-195 mg/mL) with ng detection limit and 95–106% recovery by analyzing the fluorescent signal changes caused by plasticizers (dispersive and electron transfer effects), and has highly reproducible, stable, and reproducible results. The results demonstrated that the method is highly reproducible, specific and practical [ 138 ]. However, there are still some challenges in GQDs sensor research: (1) Most of the work focuses on laboratory environment validation and lacks universal testing in complex real-world scenarios. (2) Insufficient analysis of sensing mechanisms, etc. Therefore, the future can be carried out in the following aspects: (1) technology expansion - optical properties and electrical performance synergies can be developed multi-modal sensors to enhance the detection dimension. (2) Application deepening-functionalized design can be customized with high specificity probes to promote in vivo diagnosis and food safety.

GQD for sensing applications GQDs has significant advantages in sensor applications: its excellent optical properties (strong fluorescence, broad excitation spectrum, stability) enable high-sensitivity fluorescence sensing. The large specific surface area and rich surface functional groups provide sufficient binding sites for enhanced selectivity and loading, especially for biomolecule trapping. Excellent electrical properties (high mobility, conductivity) can accelerate electron transfer and enhance the response speed and accuracy of electrochemical sensors. Good biocompatibility and low toxicity make them suitable for biomedical sensing such as cell imaging and in vivo detection. Applications of CIS QDs in different fields CIS QDs for solar cells applications CIS-based QDs offer significant advantages in solar cells: their 1.5–1.8 eV energy band structure matches the solar spectrum for efficient capture of visible-near-infrared light. Excellent carrier transport properties promote rapid photogenerated charge separation, enhancing short-circuit current and fill factor. Environmental friendliness (heavy metal free) and low-cost solution method preparation (spin coating/inkjet printing) support scale-up production. Fine tuning of size, composition, and surface ligands optimizes the energy level matching of optoelectronic devices, simultaneously enhancing performance and long-term operational reliability [ 139 – 140 ]. As a representative study, Several teams have enhanced the performance of CIS QDs solar cells through interface engineering. For example, Konstantatos et al. used formic acid ligand exchange to construct a non-annealed CIS photoconductive film in a TiO 2  porous network, and optimized the thickness of the absorber layer and carrier mobility to improve the PCE by a 7.7-fold factor, from 0.05–1.16%.The performance evolution was quantitatively verified through J-V characterization, with the corresponding curves and detailed photovoltaic parameters documented in Fig.  25  [ 141 ]。Gao et al. design TiO 2 -CIS nanorod arrays to achieve the highest efficiency of 11.7% by utilizing CIS to enhance the light trapping and electron injection capabilities [ 142 ]. Peng et al. modulated the TiO 2 /CIS photoelectrode interfacial contact by heat treatment (300℃ optimum) to promote charge separation and transfer, and PCE was improved from 4.04 to 4.68%. The photoelectric properties are characterized as shown in Fig.  26  [ 143 ].Wang et al. prepared solar cells based on CIS QDs using anatase TiO 2  nanodendrite arrays instead of nanowires, and the results showed that the CIS QDSCs were able to achieve higher current density and increase PCE from 4.7 to 5.48%, and that their photovoltaic electrodes exhibited excellent charge generation and charge separation capabilities [ 144 ]. Current research on QDSCs based on CIS QDs is still limited by (1) low absolute efficiency and enhancement dependence on specific structures. (2) High process complexity, which restricts the large-scale production. (3) The interface regulation mechanism is not fully elucidated. Therefore, in the future, the bottleneck can be broken through (1) energy band engineering to synergistically optimize light trapping and charge transport. (2) Process innovation to develop low-temperature/no annealing technology.

Highly sensitive ACP detection in the range of 0.22–12.5 U L − 1  was achieved by fluorescence “on” mode with a LOD of 0.064 U L − 1 . In addition, the designed nanosensors are biocompatible and can be successfully used for imaging and monitoring ACP levels in living cells [ 153 ]. The CIS QDs (CL) reagent was validated by employing different oxidants, and the highest CL signal was found for acidic potassium permanganate (KMnO 4 ). Based on the unique luminescence enhancement of CIS QDs/KMnO 4 , it was therefore applied as a novel CL probe for the detection of diconazole under other optimal detection conditions in the concentration range of 4.0 × 10 − 9  mol L − 1  ~ 1.5 × 10 − 6  mol L  − 1  concentration range, a linear calibration plot of diconazole was obtained [ 154 ]. Liu et al. reported a novel and simple fluorescent “switch” nanosensor based on CIS QDs for the detection of heparin and heparinase.Under the optimal conditions, the fluorescence intensity of CIS QDs showed a good linear relationship with the concentration of heparin in the range of 0.05 ~ 15 µmol L − 1  with a detection limit of 12.46 nmol L − 1 , and the linear detection range of heparinase was 0. 2 ~ 5 µmL − 1 , with a detection limit of 0.07 µmL − 1  (the fluorescence spectra of the CIS QDs in the range of different concentrations of heparin/heparinase as shown in Fig.  27 ) [ 155 ].Current research has limitations such as pressure sensing without verification of interference resistance in complex environments, biosensing limited to isolated/cellular level, and lack of empirical evidence of in vivo dynamic monitoring. Therefore, future breakthroughs need to focus on in vivo sensing-developing CIS QDs in the near-infrared-II region, coupling skull penetrating optical design, and realizing deep-tissue biomarker dynamic tracking.

Conclusion Under globally tightening environmental regulations such as the RoHS Directive and the WEEE Directive, eco-friendly QDs including InP, graphene, and CuInS₂ are poised to revolutionize biomedical, optoelectronic sensing, display, and energy-efficient lighting industries. The innovation and advancement of these QDs align with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and national green manufacturing policies, establishing regulatory prerequisites for cross-industrial adoption of environmentally compliant nanomaterials. Eco-friendly QDs exhibit distinct technological advantages. For instance, InP QDs demonstrate tunable bandgaps (emission sizes of 2.5–3.7 nm) and near-commercial external quantum efficiency (EQE > 15% in QLEDs), thus positioning them as RoHS-compliant alternatives for next-generation displays. Graphene-derived QDs meet ISO 10,993 biocompatibility standards with cytotoxicity below 5% and multimodal imaging capabilities. Meanwhile, CIS QDs achieve 60.1% PLQY using low-toxicity precursors, reducing hazardous waste by 80% compared to conventional Cd/Pb-based QDs synthesis. Since 2022, twelve eco-friendly QDs products have been certified under China’s GB/T 26,572 − 2021 standard. However, challenges persist in developing green QDs, such as QDs fluorescence imaging exhibits low sensitivity in deep-tissue in vivo applications, while metal-organic chemical synthesis of QD nanocrystals faces stringent synthesis conditions, complex reaction protocols, high costs, and abundant surface defects.

Prospect In the foreseeable future, with the continuous breakthroughs in eco-friendly QDs preparation technologies such as biological template synthesis and microwave-assisted preparation, coupled with the market forces driven by government green industry subsidies, environmental tax incentives, and other policies, the interplay and synergy of these two factors will strongly promote a profound transformation of the research paradigm in the field of nanotechnology. The in-depth exploration of cutting-edge theories by the academic community, the urgent need for technology transfer in the industrial sector, and the goal of policymakers to create a favorable development environment make strategic cooperation among the three parties the key to overcoming technical bottlenecks such as insufficient stability of QDs and difficulties in large-scale production. Specifically, by actively advancing the refinement of core-shell engineering to enhance the performance of QDs, deeply integrating the concept of circular economy to achieve efficient resource utilization and minimize waste, and simultaneously accelerating the unification and standardization of regulatory standards, it is promising to establish a green and sustainable nanotechnology ecosystem. This ecosystem will not only strictly comply with the increasingly stringent global environmental requirements but also bring transformative industrial applications to fields such as optoelectronic devices and biomedical imaging, reshaping the relevant industrial landscape and propelling global science, technology, and industry towards a greener and more efficient future.
